unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In Unit 1 you explore daily life and communication: what people do every day, and how they share their ideas. You read about routines, letters and mail, steady effort and fairness, and you meet Amal, who interviews Omar at the town post counter. You learn verb patterns, adverbs with the present simple, have got, Wh- questions, imperatives and conjunctions, using the twenty Unit 1 words. By the end you can interview someone about their work and write a fair, clear report about them.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the twenty Unit 1 words, learning one small group each day.
Work through the six grammar mini-lessons, then check your answers.
Read the three short texts and the story “Fair Effort, Daily Gains”, and answer the comprehension questions.
Work through Speaking, Writing and Activities in that order.
Finish with the unit quiz and the self-assessment.

readings.title: A Day at the Post Counter
readings.setting: Town, market and school settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript: Omar runs the market shop, and the town post counter stands beside his till. Every morning he sorts the mail, weighs the parcels, and helps people send letters. Before the market grows busy, he lines up the parcels by size and checks each address twice, because a small mistake could send a letter to the wrong street. He also reads letters aloud for neighbours who find long words difficult, sitting patiently while Grandmother Salma or old Mr Hani listens for news from a cousin far away. “Not everyone owns a phone,” he says. “A letter can bring peace and make someone feel remembered.” Omar speaks two languages, so he can serve almost every customer in town, switching smoothly between them without ever losing his patient smile. His work is not fast, but he does it with effort and care. When the shelves look crowded, he simply works a little longer instead of leaving a job half finished. Children from the school sometimes stop by after class to watch him weigh a heavy parcel or to ask what a strange stamp means. Amal is one of them; she likes to watch how carefully he checks every name before a letter leaves the counter. “Some days are busy and some are quiet, but every day matters,” Omar says, and he always closes the counter only after the last customer has gone home happy.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: My Daily Routine
readings.setting: Town, market and school settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript: Every morning I wake up early and help my mother sweep the floor and boil the water before anyone else in the house is ready. Then I fold my school clothes neatly and pack my bag, checking twice that my reading book is inside. I walk to school with my friend Maya, and we talk about our homework on the way. I usually arrive early, so I have time to greet Teacher Yasmin and put my books away calmly instead of rushing. In class we have a daily reading time, which I really like, because I can lose myself in a story for a few quiet minutes. At break I sometimes play with Sami and Theo, but I never forget that the bell will ring soon. After school I do my chores and my homework before I allow myself to rest. In the evening I try to keep a good balance between my work and my free time, so I still have a little time to draw or read for fun. If I use my time well, I can do it all, and I go to bed feeling proud of my steady, usual day.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: An Interview (script)
readings.setting: Town, market and school settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Amal: “May I interview you for my school report?”
Omar: “Of course. That sounds like a good project. Come and sit by the counter while I finish weighing this parcel.”
Amal: “Thank you! What do you do in your daily work?”
Omar: “I sort the mail, help people send letters, and serve customers. I also read letters aloud for neighbours who find long words difficult.”
Amal: “Why is mail still important?”
Omar: “Because not everyone owns a phone. A letter can make someone feel remembered.”
Amal: “Do you always work here alone?”
Omar: “Mostly, yes, but a good citizen from the market often stops to help me carry the heavier parcels.”
Amal: “How do you keep going when the shop is busy?”
Omar: “I work at a steady speed, and I never leave a job half done.”
Amal: “Is it hard to serve people who speak a different language?”
Omar: “Not for me. I learned two languages, so I can help almost anyone who comes to the counter.”
Amal: “What do you enjoy most about your usual day?”
Omar: “Watching a worried customer smile again, once their letter is safely on its way. That is worth every bit of effort.”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: Fair Effort, Daily Gains
readings.setting: Town, market and school settings familiar to learners
readings.passageScript:
Every morning, Amal helped her mother sweep the floor and boil the water before school. She liked to stay busy, because she believed that small tasks showed big effort. She also worked at a steady speed, so that she still had time to read.
At school, Teacher Yasmin pinned a notice on the classroom door. “Writing Contest!” it said. “Write a report about someone in your community. The winner gains a dictionary!”
Amal smiled. She wanted to improve her language and master new words. A dictionary would help her learn faster. She still had homework, chores and her daily reading. “I must find a balance,” she told herself. “If I use my time well, I can do it all.”
That evening her mother asked, “Can you manage this contest and your schoolwork?”
“I think so,” said Amal. “I will try my best and continue learning.”
She thought about who to write about. Many people in the town worked hard, but one stood out. Omar, the kind citizen who ran the market shop, also looked after the post counter.
After class the next day, Amal walked to the shop. “Omar,” she asked, “may I interview you for my school report?”
“Of course,” he smiled. “That sounds like a good project.”
“What do you do in your daily work?” she asked.
“I sort the mail, help people send letters, and serve customers. I also read letters for people who find long words difficult.”
“Why is mail still important?” asked Amal.
“Because not everyone owns a phone. A letter can bring peace, and it can make someone feel remembered.”
Amal asked whether he spoke more than one language. “Yes,” he said. “I had to master two languages to serve everyone here. It is necessary, so that nobody leaves the counter without help.”
“And do you do this job every day?” Amal asked.
“Yes,” he said. “It is my usual work. Some days are busy and some are quiet, but every day matters.”
Back home, Amal began her report. She wanted it to be fair and honest, so she used every detail. She checked her spelling and kept her handwriting neat.
Her father read over her shoulder. “Take your time,” he said gently. “Do not leave out anything important.”
“I won't,” she replied. “This report has a purpose.”
The next morning it rained hard. Sami ran in shouting, “The contest is cancelled!” But Teacher Yasmin said, “Nobody will cancel anything. We will hold it in the library.”
The class sat in a circle and took turns reading. Some were nervous. Nora forgot two of her lines. Amal waited quietly, and when her turn came she read clearly:
“Omar is a helpful citizen who sorts the mail and helps others read. He speaks two languages and works with care. He told me that daily effort helps us gain trust and knowledge.”
Afterwards a judge asked, “What did you learn from this?”
“I learned to listen, to write clearly, and to keep going,” Amal said with a smile.
Later that day Teacher Yasmin made the announcement. “The winner is Amal! Her report was honest, clear and full of meaning.” The whole class clapped, and Amal stood proudly with her prize, a brand-new dictionary.
At home her mother hugged her. “You did it!”
“Yes,” said Amal. “I did not stop. I worked hard, and I found a good balance.” She opened her dictionary and pointed to one word. “Look: effort means work done with care. Now I really know what it means.”

comprehension.question: Name three jobs Omar does at the post counter each morning.
comprehension.correctAnswer: He sorts the mail, weighs the parcels, and helps people send letters.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence of the text lists all three morning jobs in order.

comprehension.question: Which word in the text means calm and quiet, with no trouble?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The word is peace, which Omar says a letter can bring.
comprehension.explanation: Omar links letters to peace, so the surrounding words give the meaning away.

comprehension.question: What two jobs does the writer do at home before walking to school?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She helps her mother sweep the floor and boil the water.
comprehension.explanation: The opening sentence names both morning jobs before school is mentioned.

comprehension.question: How do we know that the writer is rarely late for school?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She writes that she usually arrives early, so lateness is not her pattern.
comprehension.explanation: The frequency adverb usually shows what normally happens, not what happened once.

comprehension.question: What reason does Omar give for saying that mail is still important?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Not everyone owns a phone, so a letter helps someone feel remembered.
comprehension.explanation: Omar answers with because, and the reason follows straight after it.

comprehension.question: Which question does Amal ask first in the interview?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She asks whether she may interview him for her school report.
comprehension.explanation: The script opens with her permission question before any work questions.

comprehension.question: What prize does Teacher Yasmin offer to the winner of the writing contest?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The winner gains a brand-new dictionary.
comprehension.explanation: The notice promises a dictionary, and Amal is holding one at the end.

comprehension.question: What happens to the contest on the wet morning, and how does Teacher Yasmin solve it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Sami shouts that it is cancelled, but Teacher Yasmin moves it into the library.
comprehension.explanation: Nothing is cancelled; the class simply reads indoors instead of outside.

comprehension.question: Why is it useful that Omar speaks two languages at the shop?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He can serve almost every customer in town, whichever language they use.
comprehension.explanation: The text puts his two languages and serving every customer in the same sentence.

comprehension.question: Which part of the school day does the writer enjoy most, and how do you know?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She enjoys the daily reading time, because she says she really likes it.
comprehension.explanation: The adverb really strengthens like, which is the writer's clearest feeling word.

comprehension.question: What does Omar mean when he calls his job his usual work?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means he does the same job every day, in a steady pattern.
comprehension.explanation: Usual describes what normally happens, and he adds that every day matters.

comprehension.question: Why does Teacher Yasmin decide that Amal's report deserves to win?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Teacher Yasmin says the report was honest, clear and full of meaning.
comprehension.explanation: The announcement gives three reasons: honesty, clarity and meaning.

grammar.title: Verb Patterns
grammar.explanation: A verb pattern is the way we join a verb to the word that follows it. Some verbs take to and another verb, and some take a verb ending in -ing. Choosing the right pattern keeps your sentences clear.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Some verbs take to and a verb: agree, want, decide, plan, need. “She agrees to send the mail.”
Some verbs take a verb with -ing: enjoy, love, like, finish. “They enjoy playing football.”
A few verbs, such as like and love, work with both patterns without changing the meaning much.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “She agrees help her friend.” ✗ Fix: agree needs to, so write “She agrees to help her friend.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Picture the main verb as a key. Some verbs carry the to key and some carry the -ing key, so learn them in pairs.
grammar.practice: Choose the correct form in brackets. | She decided ______ (to go / going) to the library. | They enjoy ______ (to play / playing) basketball. | I want ______ (to learn / learning) the second language. | He finished ______ (to write / writing) his report. | Then write one sentence of your own with agree and one with enjoy. Check yourself: 1. to go, 2. playing, 3. to learn, 4. writing. Item 5 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer — as a model, try “She agrees to help her friend” and “He enjoys reading comics.”
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Present Simple + Adverbs
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple for things we do again and again, such as checking the mail. Adverbs of frequency tell us how often, and adverbs of manner tell us how. Together they turn a plain routine sentence into one full of detail.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
For he, she and it, add -s to the verb: “He checks the mail.”
Frequency adverbs (usually, sometimes, often, rarely, never) go before the main verb: “I usually check the mail.”
With the verb to be, the frequency adverb follows it: “She is always happy.”
Manner adverbs (clearly, quickly, neatly) follow the verb or its object: “She speaks clearly.” “He checks the mail daily.”
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “He check the mail.” ✗ Fix: “He checks the mail.” ✓ Mistake: “I daily check the mail.” ✗ Fix: move the manner word to the end, “I check the mail daily.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: How often comes before the verb; how comes after it. Frequency first, manner last.
grammar.practice: Fill each blank with an adverb: daily, usually, sometimes, rarely. | I ______ go to the park at the weekend, most weeks. | She ______ reads a book before bed, but not always. | They ______ play games after school, only once in a while. | He eats breakfast every single day, so he ______ eats breakfast. | Then rewrite “She clearly speaks to the class” so the manner adverb sits after the verb. Check yourself: 1. usually, 2. sometimes, 3. rarely, 4. daily, and the rewrite is “She speaks clearly to the class.”
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Have Got and Has Got
grammar.explanation: We use have got and has got to say what someone owns or holds. It is a friendly, spoken way of talking about what people have, and it is very common in questions.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Use have got with I, you, we and they: “We have got a fair system.”
Use has got with he, she and it: “She has got the skills she needs.”
For questions, put the verb first: “Have you got the mail?”
For negatives, add not: “He has not got my letter.”
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “He have got a dog.” ✗ Fix: match the verb to the subject, so write “He has got a dog.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: have is for teams (I, you, we, they), and has is for one single player (he, she, it).
grammar.practice: Write have got or has got. | I ______ the new book. | She ______ the tidiest garden. | They ______ the same idea. | He ______ the friendliest dog. | Then turn item 4 into one question and one negative sentence. Check yourself: 1. have got, 2. has got, 3. have got, 4. has got, and item 4 becomes “Has he got the friendliest dog?” and “He has not got the friendliest dog.”
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Wh- Questions and Interview Questions
grammar.explanation: Wh- questions begin with who, what, where, when, why or how. We use them in everyday talk and in interviews, where careful questions help us understand another person's work and ideas.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Wh- word + helping verb + subject + main verb: “What do you master?”
Match the helping verb to the subject, using does for he, she and it: “What does she like?”
In an interview, add more information after the subject: “How do you gain peace in the busy shop?”
When the Wh- word is the subject, no helping verb is needed: “Who helps you at work?”
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “What do she like?” ✗ Fix: “What does she like?” ✓ Mistake: “When you leave?” ✗ Fix: add the helping verb, “When do you leave?” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Question word first, helping verb second, subject third. Keep that order and every question stays clear.
grammar.practice: Part A, fill in the correct Wh- word. | ______ is your favourite colour? | ______ do you like to do after school? | ______ does the sun set, in the morning or the evening? | ______ is your best friend? | Part B, add the question word to each interview question. | ______ do you like to eat? | ______ is your favourite subject? | ______ do you usually leave for school? | ______ can you ride a bike? Check yourself: Part A — 1. What, 2. What, 3. When, 4. Who. Part B — 1. What, 2. What, 3. When, 4. How.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Imperatives
grammar.explanation: Imperatives are command sentences that tell someone what to do. We use them for instructions, directions and polite requests, so the listener knows exactly what happens next.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Start with the base verb and leave out you: “Close the window.”
For a negative command, begin with Don't: “Don't run in the hallway.”
Add please to sound polite: “Please wash your hands.”
Chain your steps with First, Next and Then: “First, boil the water. Next, add the tea.”
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “Going to your seat!” ✗ Fix: use the base verb, so write “Go to your seat.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: In a command the verb jumps to the very front and the word you disappears.
grammar.practice: Write the correct imperative form of the verb in brackets. | ______ (close) the window, please. | ______ (not run) in the hallway. | ______ (finish) your homework before playing. | ______ (help) your brother with his project. | Then give three chained commands for making the tea. Check yourself: 1. Close, 2. Don't run, 3. Finish, 4. Help. Item 5 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer — as a model, try “First, boil the water. Next, add the tea leaves. Then, pour it into a cup.”
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Past Simple Review and Conjunctions
grammar.explanation: The past simple tells us what already happened, so we can retell a day or a story. Conjunctions then join those short past sentences into longer, smoother ones.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular past verbs add -ed: play becomes played, and walk becomes walked.
Irregular past verbs change shape: go becomes went, leave becomes left, see becomes saw, eat becomes ate.
and adds: “I read and wrote.”
but shows a difference: “I wanted to go outside, but it rained.”
or offers a choice: “Would you like cake or fruit?”
because gives a reason: “She ran fast because she had plenty of speed.”
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: “I goed to the store.” ✗ Fix: go is irregular, so write “I went to the store.” ✓ Mistake: “I wanted to go outside, and it was raining.” ✗ Fix: the two ideas are opposite, so use but. ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Add -ed and you are set, but learn the irregular verbs by heart. Conjunctions are glue: and adds, but contrasts, or chooses, because explains.
grammar.practice: Part A, write the past simple of the verb in brackets. | Yesterday, I ______ (play) outside. | They ______ (gain) speed quickly during the race. | She ______ (leave) her bike at the park. | He ______ (see) the rainbow after the rain. | Part B, join each pair with and, but, or or because. | I wanted to go to the park. It started to rain. | Would you like to play football? Would you like to play basketball? | She studies hard. She wants good marks. | I like to read books. I enjoy stories on the radio. Check yourself: Part A — 1. played, 2. gained, 3. left, 4. saw. Part B — 1. “I wanted to go to the park, but it started to rain.” 2. “Would you like to play football or basketball?” 3. “She studies hard because she wants good marks.” 4. “I like to read books, and I enjoy stories on the radio.”
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Describe Your Daily Routine
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Get ready to talk for one minute about your day. Use these sentence starters:
“Every morning I ______.”
“I usually ______ before school.”
“After school I ______, and then I ______.”
“I try to keep a balance between ______ and ______.”
Record yourself. Check: Did you use at least two adverbs (daily, usually, really, clearly)? Did you speak clearly enough to understand?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult sitting beside me, listen to my one-minute routine talk and tell me whether I used two adverbs in the right place.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Interview a Family Member
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Interview someone at home about their daily work, the way Amal interviewed Omar at the shop. Ask these four questions and note the answers:
“What do you do in your daily work?”
“Why is your work important to other people?”
“Which languages do you speak, and when do you use each one?”
“What helps you continue when the work is hard?”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play the part of the person I interview, answer my four questions in character, and afterwards tell me which question was clearest. Keep an adult with me.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Give the Instructions
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play with your AI tutor or your family, using imperatives (command sentences):
Think of a simple task, like making tea or tidying a room.
Give the steps as commands: “First, boil the water. Next, add the tea. Then, wait two minutes.”
The other person listens and repeats the steps back to you.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my chained commands for making the tea and tell me if any step is missing its base verb. An adult should be listening too.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Choose six Unit 1 words, such as balance, effort, citizen, necessary, cancel and peace. Ask a partner one clear question about each word, then answer their six questions in full sentences.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Quiz me on six Unit 1 words by asking me to use each one in a sentence, and correct any word class I get wrong while an adult listens.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Explain and Respond
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Explain why mail still matters in a town where some people own no phone. Give one reason using because, then answer two follow-up questions from your listener.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask me why mail still matters, then ask two follow-up questions and check that I gave one reason with because. An adult should be present.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Unit Talk
speaking.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Plan and record a three-minute talk called My Week. Open with one sentence about your routine, give three ideas with adverbs and examples, and close by saying how you keep a balance.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my three-minute talk, then tell me whether my opening, three ideas and closing were easy to follow. Please make sure an adult is with me.

writing.title: Writing 1: An Interview Report
writing.promptAndInstructions: Interview a person about their daily work, using your notes from Speaking 2. Then write a short, fair report about them, the way Amal wrote about Omar. Include who the person is and what they do, three things they do in their daily work, and one thing you learned from them.
writing.modelText: A strong report opens by naming the person and the job, lists three duties in order, and closes with one honest sentence about what the writer learned.
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of six to eight sentences
writing.successCriteria: I named the person and the job; I gave three duties; I used past simple for what they told me; I ended with one thing I learned; I checked capital letters and full stops
writing.support: Use your interview notes as a list, then turn each note into one sentence.
writing.extension: Add one short quotation from the person, punctuated with speech marks.

writing.title: Writing 2: My Daily Life
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a paragraph called “My Daily Life”. Use at least three adverbs, such as daily, usually, really and clearly, and join ideas with and, but or because. Finish with one sentence about how you keep a good balance.
writing.modelText: A strong paragraph moves through the day in order, places each frequency adverb before its verb, and finishes with one sentence about balance.
writing.expectedLength: One organised paragraph of six to eight sentences
writing.successCriteria: I wrote about my day in order; I used three adverbs correctly; I joined ideas with and, but or because; I finished with one balance sentence; I proofread my work
writing.support: List your day in three parts: morning, school, evening, then write one sentence for each.
writing.extension: Swap one plain verb for a stronger one, such as rushed instead of went.

writing.title: Writing 3: Why Letters Still Matter
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write six connected sentences explaining why letters and mail still matter in your town. Begin with a topic sentence and join your ideas with and, but or because.
writing.modelText: A strong answer states the main point first, gives two supporting reasons with because, and admits one difference with but.
writing.successCriteria: I opened with a topic sentence; I gave two reasons; I used because at least once; I used but to show a difference; I checked my punctuation
writing.support: Reread A Day at the Post Counter and borrow two reasons from Omar.
writing.extension: Add one sentence about what would be lost if the post counter closed.

writing.title: Writing 4: The Post Counter Fact File
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a fact file called The Post Counter. Give it a heading and five accurate facts about the work Omar does, using precise Unit 1 words such as mail, citizen, effort and peace.
writing.modelText: A strong fact file uses a clear heading, one numbered fact per line, and precise unit words instead of vague ones.
writing.expectedLength: One heading and five numbered facts
writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; I gave five separate facts; every fact is true to the text; I used four unit words; I checked my spelling
writing.support: Find one fact in each sentence of the reading, then number them.
writing.extension: Add one bulleted list of the two languages Omar uses and why.

writing.title: Writing 5: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Reread your interview report. Rewrite three sentences so they are clearer, add two useful details, and explain in one sentence what you improved and why.
writing.modelText: A strong revision shows the old sentence and the new one side by side, then names the improvement in plain words.
writing.expectedLength: Three revised sentences plus one explanation
writing.successCriteria: I chose three sentences to improve; I added two new details; I explained one change; my new sentences are easier to read; I proofread for spelling
writing.support: Read your report aloud and mark the sentence that made you pause.
writing.extension: Ask a partner to mark one more sentence, then improve that too.

writing.title: Writing 6: Instructions for a Daily Task
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write clear instructions for one daily task, such as making the tea or tidying a room. Use imperatives, number every step, and finish with one safety reminder.
writing.modelText: A strong set of instructions begins every step with a base verb, keeps the steps in order, and ends with one short safety line.
writing.expectedLength: Five numbered steps and one safety line
writing.successCriteria: Every step starts with a base verb; the steps are in order; I numbered them; I added a safety reminder; I read my steps aloud to check them
writing.support: Do the task once and say each step out loud before you write it.
writing.extension: Add one negative command using Don't to warn about a common slip.

activities.title: Activities 1: True or False
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write True or False for each sentence. If it is false, write the correct sentence.
“Daily” means something that happens once a week.
To “maintain” something means to keep it in good condition.
A “citizen” is a person who belongs to a country.
To “cancel” something means to make it happen.
activities.answerSummary: 1. False, daily means every day. 2. True. 3. True. 4. False, to cancel means to stop something from happening.

activities.title: Activities 2: Choose the Verb Pattern
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose the correct word in brackets.
She agrees ______ (to send / sending) the mail.
They enjoy ______ (to play / playing) football after school.
He wants ______ (to learn / learning) the second language.
activities.answerSummary: 1. to send 2. playing 3. to learn. Agree and want take to; enjoy takes the -ing form.

activities.title: Activities 3: Fill in the Adverb
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Fill each blank with an adverb: daily, usually, really, clearly.
I ______ check the mail every morning.
She spoke ______ so everyone could hear her.
I ______ enjoy our reading time in class.
We ______ eat lunch at noon.
activities.answerSummary: 1. daily 2. clearly 3. really 4. usually. Items 1 and 4 answer how often; items 2 and 3 answer how.

activities.title: Activities 4: Join the Sentences
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Join each pair with and, but, or because.
I write the mail. I maintain the records.
I wanted to play outside. It started to rain.
She runs fast. She has plenty of speed.
activities.answerSummary: 1. I write the mail and maintain the records. 2. I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain. 3. She runs fast because she has plenty of speed.

activities.title: Activities 5: Vocabulary Sort and Explain
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Sort these twelve words into nouns, verbs and adjectives: mail, language, citizen, effort, speed, balance, agree, continue, gain, master, daily, fair. Then write one sentence explaining the test you used for each group.
activities.answerSummary: Nouns: mail, language, citizen, effort, speed, balance. Verbs: agree, continue, gain, master. Adjectives: daily, fair. Accept any test named clearly, such as putting the in front of a noun.

activities.title: Activities 6: Reading Evidence Hunt
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Find one sentence in each of the four unit texts that shows effort, fairness, peace or daily routine. Copy the sentence and explain in one line what it tells the reader.
activities.answerSummary: Expect four copied sentences, one per text, each followed by a line naming the idea it shows and the word that carries it.

assignments.title: Daily Life & Communication learning portfolio
assignments.instructions:
Submit two pieces. First, the interview report from Writing 1, revised once using Writing 5. Second, a recording of the one-minute routine talk from Speaking 1.
Marking guidance for the teacher: award the writing marks from rub-writing-v1, looking for the person named, three duties listed, past simple used for what they said, and one honest closing sentence. Award the speaking marks from rub-speaking-v1, looking for two correctly placed adverbs, complete sentences and clear delivery. Give one written next step for each piece.
assignments.sourceFile: Derived from unit writing and speaking tasks

quizzes.question: What does the word 'peace' mean?
quizzes.options: Letters and packages that are sent or delivered. | The hard work you put into doing something. | A time when there is calm and quiet, with no fighting or trouble. | A way people talk and write to share ideas and feelings.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A time when there is calm and quiet, with no fighting or trouble.
quizzes.explanation: Peace names a calm, quiet time; the other options define mail, effort and language.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses the verb pattern after 'agree' correctly?
quizzes.options: She agrees to send the mail. | She agrees send the mail. | She agrees sending the mail tomorrow. | She agree to send the mail.
quizzes.correctAnswer: She agrees to send the mail.
quizzes.explanation: Agree takes to and a verb, and the subject she needs agrees, not agree.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'A Day at the Post Counter': Every morning he sorts the ______, weighs the parcels, and helps people send letters.
quizzes.explanation: The text says he sorts the mail, which is what arrives to be delivered.

quizzes.question: Which sentence puts the adverb of frequency in the right place?
quizzes.options: I check usually the mail. | I usually check the mail. | Usually check I the mail. | I check the mail usually not.
quizzes.explanation: Frequency adverbs sit between the subject and the main verb.

quizzes.question: Which word completes this sentence: It is ______ to wear a helmet when you ride a bike.
quizzes.explanation: Necessary means needed or very important, and the frame needs a describing word.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'balance' mean?
quizzes.options: To say that something will not happen anymore. | Having an equal, steady amount on each side. | To go away from a place. | In a way that is easy to see, hear or understand.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Having an equal, steady amount on each side.
quizzes.explanation: Balance is the steady, equal share Amal keeps between work and free time.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Fair Effort, Daily Gains': I had to ______ two languages to serve everyone here.
quizzes.explanation: Omar had to learn both languages very well, which is what master means.

quizzes.question: Which question is written correctly for an interview?
quizzes.options: When you leave for work? | What she does every day? | Why you speak two languages at work? | When do you leave for work?
quizzes.correctAnswer: When do you leave for work?
quizzes.explanation: An interview question needs its helping verb: when plus do plus you plus leave.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses a conjunction to show a difference?
quizzes.options: I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain. | She runs fast because she has plenty of speed and energy. | I write the mail and maintain the records. | Would you like football or basketball?
quizzes.correctAnswer: I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain.
quizzes.explanation: But joins two opposite ideas; because gives a reason, and adds, or offers a choice.

quizzes.question: What does the adverb 'clearly' tell us about the way someone speaks?
quizzes.options: That they speak every single day without ever missing one. | That they speak in a way that is easy to understand. | That they stop speaking before they finish. | That they speak at a very high speed.
quizzes.correctAnswer: That they speak in a way that is easy to understand.
quizzes.explanation: Clearly is an adverb of manner, so it answers how, not how often or how fast.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Launch and the first word groups
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read the unit overview and learn Group 1: mail, language, citizen, agree and continue.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min routine picture starter; 10 min teacher models the five Group 1 words; 15 min paired meaning match; 10 min sentence building with each word; 5 min set the Group 2 target
liveSessions.afterSession: Learn Group 2 and record one sentence for each of its six words.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Reading the post counter texts
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read A Day at the Post Counter and My Daily Routine, and underline any new word.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min word retrieval quiz; 10 min shared reading of the post counter text; 15 min evidence hunt in pairs; 10 min answering comprehension questions 1 to 4; 5 min sharing best evidence
liveSessions.afterSession: Finish comprehension questions 5 and 6 in full sentences.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Verb patterns and adverb placement
liveSessions.beforeSession: Work through Grammar 1 and Grammar 2, then check your answers.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min to or -ing sorting race; 10 min teacher models adverb position; 15 min guided practice from Activities 2 and 3; 10 min partners correct each other's sentences; 5 min common error round-up
liveSessions.afterSession: Rewrite four of your own sentences, moving each adverb to the right place.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Interview questions and the reading of the story
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read Fair Effort, Daily Gains and note two questions Amal asks Omar.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min question word warm-up; 10 min modelling a live interview; 15 min pairs draft four interview questions; 10 min hot-seat interviews; 5 min choosing the strongest question
liveSessions.afterSession: Interview a family member and bring your notes to the next session.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Drafting and conferencing the interview report
liveSessions.beforeSession: Bring your interview notes and a first attempt at the report opening.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min sharing one interesting answer; 10 min teacher models a fair report paragraph; 15 min independent drafting; 10 min one-to-one conferences; 5 min setting a revision target
liveSessions.afterSession: Revise three sentences and add two details, as Writing 5 asks.

liveSessions.title: Daily Life & Communication: Imperatives, presentation and reflection
liveSessions.beforeSession: Prepare your five numbered instructions from Writing 6.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min command game with base verbs; 10 min reading reports aloud; 15 min peer feedback against the rubric; 10 min unit quiz; 5 min self-assessment and next steps
liveSessions.afterSession: Complete the unit quiz and the self-assessment, then set one target for Unit 2.

teacherNotes.note: Model each new pattern aloud and check meaning before independent work, then give feedback on complete sentences, text evidence and precise vocabulary. An adult must be present whenever a learner uses the AI tutor or records audio; never leave a child alone with the device. Offer spoken answers as an alternative to written ones for learners who need it.

Suggested tutor prompts, drawn from the four source files and to be used with a caregiver sitting alongside.
Reading: ask the tutor to read the interview script with you and take the part of Omar.
Vocabulary: ask for one more example sentence for any word you find hard, and for the difference between agree and continue.
Grammar: ask why we say she likes but I like, and for five more verb pattern sentences.
Speaking: ask the tutor to be the person you interview and to answer your four questions.
Writing: ask the tutor to check whether your report is clear and fair, and whether your conjunctions are used correctly.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Peace. The other three options define mail, effort and language, so a learner who mixes them needs another meaning-match round.
She agrees to send the mail. Watch for learners who fix the -s but keep the wrong pattern.
Mail. If a learner picks citizen, reread the sentence and point to sorts, which needs a thing, not a person.
I usually check the mail. Ask the learner to point to the subject and the main verb, then place the adverb between them.
Necessary. The gap needs a describing word, so a verb such as cancel cannot fit the frame.
Having an equal, steady amount on each side. Link this back to Amal saying she must find a balance.
Master. If a learner chooses continue, reread the whole line: Omar had already learned both languages.
When do you leave for work? Ask the learner to say the helping verb aloud before writing the question.
I wanted to play outside, but it started to rain. Check that the learner can also say why because does not fit here.
That they speak in a way that is easy to understand. Clearly answers how, so option 4 about speed is the useful discussion point.
